schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch lay out the chapter's whole plan — securing the walls, then peopling the city, then ordering civil life — and extend the doorkeepers' ancient charge over God's house to the city watch.
Henry hears God's word 'I have set watchmen upon thy walls' (Isa. 62:6): dead walls without living watchmen are a poor defence, and God's worship is itself the defence of a place.
Gill marks that the doors were now set up, the fortification of Jerusalem complete only after Sanballat's earlier threats.
Clarke sets the verse at the head of the chapter's business — guarding the gates, then reckoning the people by genealogy.

themes: the wall built and the doors set up
worship the defence of a place
except the Lord keep the city

schools.summary: Clarke reads the appointment against Nehemiah's coming absence and finds in Hananiah the two marks of a governor — faithful, and fearing God above many.
Henry: faithful in less, entrusted with more; among those who fear God some fear him greatly (Ps. 15:4), worthy of double honour.
Keil corrects the Chethiv to the Keri ('I gave charge') and sets out the watch of posts and houses.
Gill identifies Hanani as the brother who first brought news of Jerusalem's ruin (Neh. 1:2), and Hananiah as ruler of the palace.

themes: a faithful man who feared God above many
integrity as the city's true defence

schools.summary: Clarke fixes the eastern custom — gates opened only after sunrise, shut at sunset, latecomers lodging outside — and every man guarding the wall opposite his house; Wesley glosses 'sun be hot' as clear, broad day.
Gill takes 'until the sun be hot' of the heat of the day, that lurking enemies be seen by daylight and the inhabitants be ready.

themes: the gates opened only by day
every one over against his house
the eastern custom of the gates

schools.summary: Keil renders 'broad on both sides,' and reads the clause not that there were no houses (the city was 90 years re-inhabited) but that it was under-built, with room to fill.
Henry: Nehemiah walled the city in faith, eyeing Zechariah's promise of a replenished Jerusalem (Zech. 8:3), building large for a people not yet come.
Gill dwells on the compass of the city — Hecataeus's fifty furlongs, Josephus's thirty-three — the wall rebuilt on the old foundation.

themes: room prepared against a coming multitude

schools.summary: Keil: God inspired the resolution (cf. Neh. 2:12) to enrol the people; the register Nehemiah found, of those who came up first under Cyrus, is identical with the roll in Ezra 2.
Henry: 'my God put it into my heart' — every good motion is from God; a city's safety lies more in its people than its walls; God knows his own by name.
Clarke and Wesley alike: with this good man every good thing was of God, and whatever good motion is in our minds must be acknowledged to come from him.
Gill: Nehemiah always ascribed to God every good thought for Jerusalem's welfare.

themes: God put it into my heart
the enrolment for peopling the city
the register of the first return
every good motion is from God

schools.summary: Keil calls the list identical with Ezra 2 — the children of the province carried off by Nebuchadnezzar, now home each to his city; he and Ellicott take many divergences for copyists' slips.
Gill explains the differences by two reckonings — Ezra's made in Babylon, this at Jerusalem — some enrolling then dying or staying, others joining later.
Wesley refers the divergences to multiple names and to changes over the years; Clarke to his three copies (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esdras) correcting one another.
Henry: the repetition of the roll shows God's delight in his people, whom he knows by name.

debates.question: Why do the numbers and names of this register differ from the parallel in Ezra 2?

sides.position: two separate reckonings — Ezra's taken in Babylon, this one at Jerusalem, with deaths, defaults, and late-comers between
the same persons bore several names, and families changed over the intervening years
the three copies (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esdras) correct one another, surplus reconciling shortfall
ordinary clerical and transcription errors of a hand-copied document

themes: God knows his own by name

schools.summary: Clarke fastens on the Tirshatha whose gift heads the offering, citing the Codex Alexandrinus and referring to Ezra 2:63 for the title.
Gill: the chief fathers gave toward the building of city and temple and its service.

Henry: this account differs from Ezra 2:68 (the Tirshatha here beginning), yet is probably the same contribution from a different copy — faith rests not on niceties of numbers but on the great things of the gospel.

debates.question: Is this offering the same as the one recorded in Ezra 2:68-69?

sides.position: probably the same contribution, one historian following one copy of the lists and the other another
another and later collection than the first, hence the differing sums

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott judge Nehemiah's own statement of the gifts more exact than the parallel, supposing round numbers in Ezra 2:69 to have suffered in copying.
Clarke checks the silver against the Septuagint (2,300 minae) and sees God's mercy that a people carried off with nothing came home able to give so much.
Gill: the gold and silver were laid up in the treasure to defray the temple's expenses.
Henry: given by drams, not talents as in David's day, yet as acceptable as the widow's two mites.
Gill reckons the people's gold at twenty thousand drachms, worth as many pounds and more.
Wesley explains the difference from Ezra 2:69 by the Tirshatha's part and this being another, later collection.
Henry: given by drams, not the talents of David's day (1 Chron. 29:7), yet acceptable as the widow's two mites — the whole nation sharing the gift.

themes: what the rest of the people gave

schools.summary: Ellicott hears triumph in 'all Israel in their cities' — no partial affair but a national revival, though Judah and Benjamin furnished the most.
Clarke: the registers determined the cities, the wall finished in Elul (Neh. 6:15) and the families settled by Tisri, leaving no room for complaint; Wesley marks their peace and perfect unity.
Gill: the cities were those assigned them, where they or their forefathers had dwelt before the captivity.
Henry: content in their ruined but assigned cities, room enough and no strife — the homecoming a shadow of the gospel return to the holy city of God.

themes: the homecoming a shadow of the gospel

schools.summary: Ellicott: the leaders, twelve for the twelve tribes, stood defective in Ezra 2 (Nahamani dropped, three names altered); here the twelfth name is restored.

Clarke: the register was of the earlier return and only partly altered by Nehemiah, hence its differences from Ezra; Wesley: the Tirshatha here is Nehemiah, the later collection differing from Ezra 2:68.
Gill takes Jeshua for Joshua the high priest and judges the Nehemiah and Mordecai here different men from the famous ones.
Henry makes Zerubbabel and Jeshua the Moses and Aaron of the return and thinks Nehemiah and Mordecai probably the same famous men.

debates.question: Are the Nehemiah and Mordecai among the leaders the famous men of those names?

sides.position: probably the same famous men, come now and afterward returned to their work
rather different men of the same names, the famous Nehemiah belonging to a later reign

schools.summary: Clarke refers the reader to Ezra 2 and lays down the rule — 'children' before a man means descendants, before a place inhabitants; Wesley fixes 'children of Parosh' as his posterity.
Ellicott opens his family-by-family comparison, Parosh's 2,172 agreeing in all copies (Ezra 2:3); Keil confirms it in parallel columns.
Gill: the captives are set down by ancestor or town and by number, most otherwise unknown.
Henry finds it good that a restored people should remember their small beginnings and own God in multiplying them, the genealogies kept until the Messiah should come.

themes: a number agreeing in all copies

schools.summary: Clarke notes the copies (2,067 here, 2,056 in Ezra 2:14, some MSS 2,066) correcting one another; Wesley explains the gap as those who set out from Babylon versus those who arrived.
Keil and Ellicott take such variations for the ordinary slips of a hand-copied text, weighing the copies without forcing a reconciliation.

debates.question: How is the divergence between this register's number and Ezra's to be explained?

sides.position: the difference between those who marched out of Babylon and those who reached Jerusalem
clerical and transcription errors of a hand-copied document
the three copies correcting one another, surplus reconciling shortfall

outliers.note: Explains the numeric divergence from Ezra as the difference between those who set out from Babylon and those who arrived at Jerusalem, offered once for all such cases.

schools.summary: Clarke notes 'other' is wanting in Ezra 2:29 and in many MSS, takes Nebo for Nob/Nobah in Benjamin, and reads its 'men' as the town's inhabitants.
Keil and Ellicott take the added or dropped word for the ordinary variation of a hand-copied text, the number (52) agreeing.
Gill keeps the frame — captives named by ancestor or town, most otherwise unknown.

themes: the men of the other Nebo
a single word varying between the copies

schools.summary: Clarke: 'the other Elam' is so styled to distinguish this house from the Elam of v.12, the two bearing one name and one number; and 'children' before the name marks descendants of a man.
Keil records the second Elam at 1,254, the same in Ezra 2:31, and hands down the duplicate figure unaltered.
Gill sets it among the houses known only by name and number.
Henry: the very repetition of the roll betokens God's delight in his people and his knowledge of them house by house.

themes: two houses of one name and one number

schools.summary: Clarke notes many MSS read Mehira for Mehida, the parallel (Ezra 2:52) carrying the same cluster with small differences of spelling; Wesley fixes the Nethinim as devoted to the inferior services.
Keil counts them among the 35 Nethinim households (392 in all), the parallel now agreeing and now diverging in the form of the words.
Gill keeps them the descendants of the Gibeonites, only bare names now surviving.
Henry: an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office there.

themes: little families of the given ones

schools.summary: Gill reads the few horses and mules as a mark of poverty, most of the people walking home on foot.
Clarke turns the tally to praise — a people once stripped now returning abounding in riches — and notes the verse wanting in many MSS but secure in Ezra 2:66.
Keil notes the beasts stand at identical figures in both registers, where the counts of men so often part.
Keil notes the camels and asses at the same figures as Ezra 2:67; Ellicott marks the ass throughout Hebrew history the chief and most numerous beast of burden.
Clarke keeps the note of returning riches and records Jerome's Latin addition after the verse, absent from Hebrew and the versions.

themes: the ass the beast of burden

schools.summary: Keil records Elam at 1,254, the same in Ezra 2:7; Ellicott reckons it among the agreeing entries that fix the document's shape.

Clarke notes the same name and number recur at v.34 as 'the other Elam,' the qualifier distinguishing two houses, and keeps his three-copies reconciliation; Wesley reads the head-name as a father, the children his posterity.
Gill sets Elam among the houses known only by ancestor and number.
Henry gives the dry entry its worth — the account an honour to the families and a benefit to their posterity, God knowing them by name.

themes: the register an honour to posterity

schools.summary: Wesley's principle — several names given to the same persons — meets a clear instance, Hariph here and Jorah in Ezra 2:18 for one house of 112; Clarke's rule marks it a personal, not a place, name.
Keil and Ellicott treat the differing names as the marks of a text long copied by hand, the steady number proving the one company.
Gill keeps the roll's character, families named by ancestor or town, most otherwise unknown.

debates.question: How is a house appearing under two different names (Hariph here, Jorah in Ezra) to be understood?

sides.position: the same persons bore several names — one family under two
a scribal variant of a long-copied text, the unchanging number fixing the identity

themes: a name that varies, a number that holds

schools.summary: Keil counts these among the 35 Nethinim families (with 10 of Solomon's servants, 392 in all, 8-9 to a clan) and notes the variant forms (Shalmai/Salmai/Shamlai) against Ezra 2:44.
Gill takes the Nethinim for the Gibeonites, given by Joshua (Josh. 9:27) and David to serve the house — 'the given ones.'
Wesley calls them persons devoted to the inferior services of the priests and Levites.
Henry: an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office there.

Keil sums 35 Nethinim families and 10 of Solomon's servants at 392 (8-9 to a family), the same total as Ezra 2:58; Ellicott makes Solomon's servants the remnant of the Canaanites (1 Kings 9:21), faithful to their service.
Wesley: they had lived in Solomon's household and gloried afterward in the name of servants to so great a prince.
Henry: an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office there.
